title: Gargi, the woman who asked: on what is water woven? (3.6)
hook: a woman stands up in a courtyard full of men and asks a child's endless why, at the scale of the universe
tomorrow: Uddalaka: the thread and the inner controller

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kahola asked Ushasta's question again, and heard: beyond hunger, grief and death; after learning, live like a child. Your line was beyond.

Why is it raining? Because of the clouds. Why are there clouds? Because of the water. Why is there water? A child can keep that chain going until the grown-up says, because I said so. Now put that chain in a royal courtyard, where a woman has just stood up among the learned men of the Kuru and Panchala lands. Her name is Gargi Vachaknavi, and she's about to ask Yajnavalkya why, again and again, all the way to the top.
screen: `WHY? AND WHY THAT?` → `A WOMAN STANDS UP.` → `ALL THE WAY TO THE TOP.`

segments.voice: Yajnavalkya, she says, everything here is woven, back and forth, on water. On what, then, is water woven? Weaving is her picture: threads running lengthwise and crosswise, each one held by another. On wind, Gargi, he says. On what is wind woven? On the worlds of the middle air. On what are those woven? On the worlds of the heavenly musicians. Then the worlds of the sun. Of the moon. Of the stars. Of the gods. Of Indra. Of Prajapati, the lord of creatures. And on what are the worlds of Prajapati woven? On the worlds of Brahman. On what, she asks, are the worlds of Brahman woven? Here he stops her. Gargi, don't ask too much, or your head will fall off. You are asking too far about a deity one shouldn't ask beyond. And Gargi falls silent. It's a startling moment. The same warning comes up more than once in this book, and here it marks the place where argument stops. Every answer so far named a thing, and you can always ask what holds a thing. But what holds everything isn't one more thread in the cloth. Asking what it's woven on is like asking what's north of the North Pole. Gargi isn't wrong to ask. She's found the edge of the question. And she isn't finished. In two days, she'll stand up again, and this time she'll come armed.
screen: `ON WHAT IS WATER WOVEN?` · `WIND, AIR, SUN, MOON, STARS, GODS.` · `DON'T ASK TOO MUCH, GARGI.` · `THE EDGE OF THE QUESTION.` · then, large: `THE WEAVE.`

segments.voice: Feel what holds you: you on the seat, the seat on the floor, the floor on the building, the building on the earth, the earth held in space, with a breath at each step. When you reach the last one you can name, don't push for another. Rest right there, at the edge, where the answers stop and you're still held.
Gargi. The woman who asked what everything is woven on, ota and prota, warp and weft, until the answers ran out at the edge of the question.
Your line: the weave. Tomorrow, an old friend from the Chandogya steps up. That's day three hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Hindu tradition remembers Gargi Vachaknavi as a philosopher of the Vedic age, and her questions to Yajnavalkya are studied as part of the Brihadaranyaka's great debate.

original.note: Sanskrit ota and prota: woven lengthwise and crosswise, warp and weft, from vā, to weave.

trapdoor: what you thought: Gargi was silenced for asking too much.
what it means: she followed the chain of what holds what to its edge, where what holds everything isn't one more thread.
what a scholar hears: ota-prota, warp and weft (3.6.1); 'your head will fall off' is a warning heard more than once in the Brihadaranyaka's debates, and Gargi returns in 3.8.

chat.says: Why did Yajnavalkya stop Gargi's questions? Was she asking something wrong?
options: No, she'd reached the edge: what holds everything isn't one more thread to ask about.
Yes, she was trying to trick him with a riddle, so he refused to answer it.
No, he'd already answered it earlier, so there was no need to repeat himself.
chat.meaning: Each answer named a thing, but what holds everything isn't one more thread. Gargi isn't wrong to ask; she's found the edge of the question.

Gargi Vachaknavi.meaning: a woman philosopher who questions Yajnavalkya

Kuru.meaning: an ancient people of northern India

Panchala.meaning: an ancient people, neighbors of the Kurus

Brahman.meaning: the ultimate reality, the ground of everything

ota.meaning: woven lengthwise; with prota, warp and weft

notes: Sequence in 3.6.1: water → wind → atmosphere worlds → gandharva worlds → sun worlds → moon worlds → star worlds → god worlds → Indra's worlds → Prajapati's worlds → Brahman's worlds. Confirm.
The warning (mā te mūrdhā vyapaptat; 'a deity beyond which one should not ask', anatipraśnyā devatā) is paraphrased.
'One of very few women named as philosophers in the Vedic texts': Gargi and Maitreyi are the usual examples; confirm the phrasing.
The 'north of the North Pole' analogy is the writer's own illustration, not the text's.
